content: A cube is a three-dimensional geometric solid that is enclosed by six square faces. At each vertex, three of these square faces meet. The cube is also referred to as a regular hexahedron and is one of the five Platonic solids. It is a specific type of square prism, rectangular parallelepiped, and 3-sided trapezohedron. The cube is geometrically dual to the octahedron and exhibits cubical symmetry, which is also known as octahedral symmetry. In a broader mathematical context, a cube is the three-dimensional instance of a hypercube, a concept that can be extended to any number of dimensions. If a cube is centered at the origin in a Cartesian coordinate system, with its edges aligned parallel to the coordinate axes and an edge length of 2, the vertices of the cube can be described using specific Cartesian coordinates. The interior of the cube consists of all points (x₀, x₁, x₂) that satisfy the condition -1 < xᵢ < 1 for each coordinate xᵢ. The volume of a cube is calculated as the cube of its edge length, expressed as (a times a times a), where (a) is the edge length. This is why the term cube is used to describe the third power of a number, analogous to how square is used for the second power. Among all cuboids (rectangular boxes) with a given surface area, the cube has the largest possible volume. Similarly, for cuboids with the same total linear dimensions (sum of length, width, and height), the cube also maximizes volume. The cube has three distinct classes of symmetry. The highest level of symmetry, known as octahedral symmetry (Oh), is achieved when all six faces of the cube are the same color. A lower level of symmetry, dihedral symmetry (D4h), arises when the cube is treated as a prism, with four of its sides sharing the same color. The lowest symmetry class, D2h, is another prismatic symmetry where the cube's sides alternate in color, resulting in three distinct colors paired across opposite faces. Each symmetry class corresponds to a unique Wythoff symbol. The cube is unique among the Platonic solids because it can tile three-dimensional space regularly. It is also the only Platonic solid with faces that have an even number of sides, making it a zonohedron, a polyhedron where every face exhibits point symmetry. In four-dimensional Euclidean space, the analogue of a cube is called a tesseract or, less commonly, a hypercube. Lower-dimensional analogues of the cube include a point in zero dimensions, a line segment in one dimension, and a square in two dimensions. The vertices of a cube can be divided into two groups of four, each forming a regular tetrahedron. Together, these two tetrahedra create a regular compound known as the stella octangula. The intersection of these two tetrahedra forms a regular octahedron. The symmetries of a regular tetrahedron correspond to those of a cube that map the tetrahedron onto itself, while other cube symmetries map one tetrahedron onto the other. A single regular tetrahedron occupies one-third of the cube's volume, while the remaining space is divided into four equal irregular polyhedra, each with a volume of one-sixth of the cube. A rectified cube, also known as a cuboctahedron, is formed by truncating the vertices of a cube. If the truncation is extended further, a polyhedron with six octagonal faces and eight triangular faces is produced, which can include regular octagons in the case of a truncated cube. The rhombicuboctahedron is created by truncating both the vertices and edges of the cube to a specific degree. A cube can also be inscribed within a dodecahedron such that each vertex of the cube coincides with a vertex of the dodecahedron, and each edge of the cube corresponds to a diagonal of one of the dodecahedron's faces. This arrangement gives rise to the regular compound of five cubes. The cube is associated with several related polyhedra, including the stella octangula, the cuboctahedron, the truncated cube, the rhombicuboctahedron, and the compound of three cubes. All of these polyhedra, except for the alternately truncated cube, share the same symmetries as the cube, specifically octahedral symmetry. In graph theory, a different interpretation of the cube exists as the cube graph, which represents the vertices and edges of the geometric cube. This graph is a specific case of the hypercube graph. An extension of this concept is the three-dimensional k-ary Hamming graph, which reduces to the cube graph when k = 2. Such graphs are significant in the study of parallel processing in computer science.
